newsitem.title: USA: EDS reports higher profits, but outlook hits stock.
newsitem.headline: EDS reports higher profits, but outlook hits stock.

text.p: Electronic Data Systems Corp., the giant computer services firm founded by billionaire Ross Perot 34 years ago, stunned Wall Street on Wednesday when it warned of sharply slower growth in the fourth quarter.
EDS, based in Plano, Texas, blamed the slowdown on a drop in new business contracts signed so far this year and an expected decline in government spending.
The warning sent the company's stock tumbling almost 20 percent to $48, down $11.50 on the New York Stock Exchange, despite its reporting stronger sales and profits for the third quarter.

Investors are used to EDS posting steady growth of 15 percent or more, but senior executives warned of a sharp decline to low double-digit or high single-digit growth in the last three months of the year.
Founded in 1962 with an investment of $1,000 by Perot, EDS said it won just $5.37 billion in new business so far this year, compared with $6.58 billion in the same period of 1995.
Analysts said they were shocked by the warning, and that company executives did not succeed in calming their nerves during a two-hour conference call.

"The management team could not give the Street a whole lot of comfort that this was the last earnings cut," said Hugh Shytle from Cowen and Co., adding that he dropped his earnings projections for the full year and 1997.

For the third quarter ended in September -- the first full quarter since EDS was spun off in June by General Motors Corp. -- EDS said it earned $266.4 million, or 55 cents a share, up from $245.7 million, or 51 cents a share in the same period of 1995. Sales rose 16 percent to $3.57 billion from $3.07 billion.

The profit, while in line with Wall Street's consensus estimate of 55 cents a share, was quickly overshadowed by the company's fourth-quarter warning and news that one of its customers that filed for bankruptcy earlier this month owed EDS $24 million.

Memorex Telex Corp. an EDS customer, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on Oct. 15 and said it was seeking to liquidate and sell its U.S. assets. EDS said it was too early to determine the amount of its recovery, if any, in the bankruptcy proceeding.

Chief Financial Officer Jody Grant said the government spending cutback would likely hurt EDS on four "indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity" contracts that were expected to bring in about $400 million in revenue this year.

But Grant said the third quarter saw a sharp increase in new contracts over the first half of the year, and that he was confident looking forward to 1997. "In terms of total contract value, the pipeline is very full ... It is as robust and as big as we've seen it."
Grant said he was puzzled by the sharp drop in EDS' stock price, and attributed it to a knee-jerk reaction from a volatile stock market.

Some analysts agreed. "This kind of overreaction opens up a good buying opportunity," said Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford, Brown and Catherwood. "Government spending is down more than I had anticipated and they may be feeling some pressure from GM and others, but, long-term, I think the outlook is excellent," Brown said.
Company executives stressed that the fourth-quarter results would in part look worse simply because the last quarter of 1995 was the best in the company's history.
For the first nine months of 1996, EDS earned $158 million, or 33 cents a share, on revenue of $10.43 billion. A year earlier, it earned $669 million, or $1.40 a share, on sales of $8.80 billion.
The 1996 period included a one-time charge of $850 million, or $1.12 a share, which EDS described in June as related to realigning its operations.
